--- title: "Finding the parameters" description: "Linear regression's parameters come from a formula in one step; almost every other model searches for them. A search that went wrong still prints coefficients, so check that it finished." order: 2 categories: [optimisation] --- {{< new-terms >}} ## Parameters are solved in one step or found by searching [Loss functions](loss-functions.qmd) gave each fit a number to make as small as possible. This page shows the two ways a model finds the parameter values that do it. Linear regression has a formula that gives them exactly, in one step. Every other model in [Supervised learning](../03-supervised-learning/index.qmd) has to search for them, and a search can stop too early or walk off without finding an answer, while still printing coefficients that look normal. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## The fit sets parameters and you set hyperparameters A **parameter** is a number the fit chooses from the data: a slope in a regression, or the value a decision tree splits at. You do not set these. A hyperparameter, met on [k-nearest neighbours](../03-supervised-learning/nearest-neighbours.qmd), is the opposite: a setting fixed before fitting, such as the number of neighbours or the depth of a tree. The fit cannot choose it, because its job is to limit what the fit may do, so it is chosen on validation data; [Hyperparameter selection](../05-generalisation/hyperparameter-selection.qmd) shows how. ::: {.callout-note} ## "Parameter" means different things in different fields In this course a parameter is always a number the fit estimates from the data. Marine science often uses the word differently, so check which meaning a paper or a help page has in mind. - **Oceanography and water-quality monitoring** call the measured variables parameters: temperature, salinity, oxygen and nutrients are "hydrographic parameters". In this course those are [inputs](../01-introduction/types-of-learning.qmd) or the outcome, never parameters. - **Population and stock-assessment models** call any constant in the model a parameter, including ones fixed from the literature, such as natural mortality, rather than estimated from the data at hand. - **Statistics** reserves the word for a property of the population, such as the true mean, and calls the fitted value its estimate. - **scikit-learn** calls the settings you pass to a model its parameters, so what this course calls hyperparameters come back from `get_params()`. The values it learns end in an underscore, as in `coef_`. ::: ## Fitting finds the lowest point of a landscape For a straight line, the objective depends on two parameters, the intercept and the slope. Draw it as a map, with the two parameters as the axes and the objective as the height, and fitting means finding the lowest point. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() d <- survey |> select(abundance, chlorophyll_mg_m3) |> drop_na() grid <- expand_grid( intercept = seq(-2, 6, length.out = 120), slope = seq(-1, 3, length.out = 120) ) |> mutate(mse = map2_dbl( intercept, slope, \(a, b) mean((d$abundance - (a + b * d$chlorophyll_mg_m3))^2) )) best <- coef(lm(abundance ~ chlorophyll_mg_m3, data = d)) ggplot(grid, aes(intercept, slope, fill = mse)) + geom_raster() + geom_contour(aes(z = mse), colour = "white", alpha = 0.35, bins = 14) + annotate("point", x = best[1], y = best[2], shape = 4, size = 4, stroke = 1.2, colour = "white") + scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "viridis", trans = "log10") + labs( x = "Intercept", y = "Slope", fill = "Mean squared\nerror (log scale)", title = "The objective for a straight line is a bowl" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The mean squared error of a straight line of abundance against chlorophyll, for every intercept and slope on a grid. Darker is lower. The surface is a long, tilted bowl with one lowest point, marked by the cross at an intercept of 2.36 and a slope of 1.15.](parameter-estimation_files/figure-html/fig-surface-1.png){#fig-surface fig-alt='A filled contour plot with intercept on the horizontal axis from minus two to six and slope on the vertical axis from minus one to three. The colour shades from yellow at the edges to dark blue in a narrow valley running diagonally from upper left to lower right. A white cross marks the single lowest point, at an intercept of 2.36 and a slope of 1.15.' width=1300} ::: ::: ::: The bowl has one lowest point, so every way downhill ends there. It is also long and narrow: along the diagonal valley, a higher intercept with a lower slope fits almost as well, so the data pin down some combinations of the two far better than others. That shape matters on [Gradient descent](gradient-descent.qmd). The figure found the lowest point by trying every combination on a grid, 120 values for each parameter. That works for two parameters and fails soon after. At 100 values each, two parameters make ten thousand combinations, done in a moment; four make a hundred million; ten make $10^{20}$, which at a billion a second takes about 3,200 years. Real fits use the shape of the objective instead, in one of three ways. ::: {.diagram} ![Linear regression's parameters come from a formula in one step. Poisson and logistic regression search step by step downhill until the objective stops falling. Trees, forests and boosting choose one split at a time and never revisit it.](img/finding-parameters.svg){fig-alt="Three cards. By formula, solved in one step, linear regression: an arrow labelled solve points straight down to the lowest point of a U-shaped objective curve; exact, and the same answer every time. By search, step by step downhill, Poisson and logistic regression: a row of dots from a point marked start steps down the curve, each step shorter, to its lowest point; repeats until the objective stops falling. One split at a time, greedy, trees, forests and boosting: a small tree with its first and second splits filled in; takes the best split now and never goes back to it. A note says a search can stop early or end somewhere else; a formula cannot."} ::: ## Worked example ### Linear regression has a formula For linear regression under squared error, algebra gives the lowest point of the bowl directly: the **normal equations**, solved once. We fit abundance on chlorophyll, depth and temperature this way and compare with `lm()`. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} d3 <- survey |> select(abundance, chlorophyll_mg_m3, depth_m, temperature_c) |> drop_na() X <- model.matrix(~ chlorophyll_mg_m3 + depth_m + temperature_c, data = d3) y <- d3$abundance by_formula <- drop(solve(t(X) %*% X, t(X) %*% y)) by_lm <- coef(lm(abundance ~ chlorophyll_mg_m3 + depth_m + temperature_c, data = d3)) tibble(term = names(by_lm), `by formula` = by_formula, `by lm()` = by_lm) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 4))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|term | by formula| by lm()| |:-----------------|----------:|-------:| |(Intercept) | 5.1170| 5.1170| |chlorophyll_mg_m3 | 1.0265| 1.0265| |depth_m | -0.0159| -0.0159| |temperature_c | -0.1313| -0.1313|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import warnings import numpy as np import pandas as pd import statsmodels.api as sm from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, LogisticRegression from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() inputs = ["chlorophyll_mg_m3", "depth_m", "temperature_c"] d3 = survey[["abundance", *inputs]].dropna() X = sm.add_constant(d3[inputs]).to_numpy() y = d3["abundance"].to_numpy() by_formula = np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X, X.T @ y) line = LinearRegression().fit(d3[inputs], y) pd.DataFrame({ "term": ["intercept", *inputs], "by formula": by_formula, "by LinearRegression": [line.intercept_, *line.coef_], }).round(4) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | term | by formula | by LinearRegression | |:------------------|-------------:|----------------------:| | intercept | 5.117 | 5.117 | | chlorophyll_mg_m3 | 1.0265 | 1.0265 | | depth_m | -0.0159 | -0.0159 | | temperature_c | -0.1313 | -0.1313 | ::: ::: ::: The two agree: the largest difference is 8e-14, rounding error in the last digits a computer stores. `lm()` solves the same equations by a route that is safer with awkward data. There is no starting value and nothing to converge, so the answer is the same on every run. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## The maths, if you want it With $X$ the table of inputs (one row per station, plus a column of ones for the intercept), $y$ the observed values and $\beta$ the coefficients, the objective is the sum of squared residuals, $\lVert y - X\beta \rVert^2$. Its lowest point is where its slope in every direction is zero, which gives $$X^\top X \hat\beta = X^\top y \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \hat\beta = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top y$$ This works because squaring makes the objective a bowl whose lowest point can be solved for. Absolute error has no such formula, which is why [Loss functions](loss-functions.qmd) needed `optim()` for it. ::: ### Logistic regression searches until it stops improving [Logistic regression](../03-supervised-learning/logistic-regression.qmd) has no formula for its lowest point, so `glm()` finds it by repeating one step. Each step replaces the objective with a weighted linear regression that matches it near the current coefficients, solves that by formula, and starts again from the answer. We write the steps out, starting from coefficients of zero, and watch the objective, the mean log loss from [Loss functions](loss-functions.qmd#counts-and-presence-have-their-own-losses). ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} d3b <- survey |> select(present, chlorophyll_mg_m3, depth_m, temperature_c) |> drop_na() |> mutate(present = fct_relevel(present, "no")) Xb <- model.matrix(~ chlorophyll_mg_m3 + depth_m + temperature_c, data = d3b) yb <- as.numeric(d3b$present == "yes") log_loss <- function(b) { eta <- drop(Xb %*% b) -mean(yb * eta - log1p(exp(eta))) } b <- rep(0, ncol(Xb)) start <- log_loss(b) steps <- map_dfr(1:6, function(k) { eta <- drop(Xb %*% b) p <- plogis(eta) w <- p * (1 - p) z <- eta + (yb - p) / w b <<- drop(solve(t(Xb) %*% (Xb * w), t(Xb) %*% (w * z))) tibble(step = k, log_loss = log_loss(b), chlorophyll = b[2], depth = b[3], temperature = b[4]) }) steps |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 5))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| step| log_loss| chlorophyll| depth| temperature| |----:|--------:|-----------:|--------:|-----------:| | 1| 0.51047| 0.12764| -0.00259| 0.00323| | 2| 0.50373| 0.26844| -0.00342| 0.00185| | 3| 0.50323| 0.33997| -0.00339| -0.00034| | 4| 0.50322| 0.34809| -0.00338| -0.00064| | 5| 0.50322| 0.34817| -0.00338| -0.00064| | 6| 0.50322| 0.34817| -0.00338| -0.00064|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} d3b = survey[["present", *inputs]].dropna() Xb = sm.add_constant(d3b[inputs]).to_numpy() yb = (d3b["present"] == "yes").to_numpy(dtype=float) def log_loss(b): eta = Xb @ b return -np.mean(yb * eta - np.log1p(np.exp(eta))) b = np.zeros(Xb.shape[1]) start = log_loss(b) rows = [] for step in range(1, 7): eta = Xb @ b p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-eta)) w = p * (1 - p) z = eta + (yb - p) / w b = np.linalg.solve(Xb.T @ (Xb * w[:, None]), Xb.T @ (w * z)) rows.append({"step": step, "log_loss": log_loss(b), "chlorophyll": b[1], "depth": b[2], "temperature": b[3]}) steps = pd.DataFrame(rows) steps.round(5) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | step | log_loss | chlorophyll | depth | temperature | |-------:|-----------:|--------------:|---------:|--------------:| | 1 | 0.51047 | 0.12764 | -0.00259 | 0.00323 | | 2 | 0.50373 | 0.26844 | -0.00342 | 0.00185 | | 3 | 0.50323 | 0.33997 | -0.00339 | -0.00034 | | 4 | 0.50322 | 0.34809 | -0.00338 | -0.00064 | | 5 | 0.50322 | 0.34817 | -0.00338 | -0.00064 | | 6 | 0.50322 | 0.34817 | -0.00338 | -0.00064 | ::: ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} glm_fit <- glm(present ~ chlorophyll_mg_m3 + depth_m + temperature_c, data = d3b, family = binomial) round(coef(glm_fit), 5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> (Intercept) chlorophyll_mg_m3 depth_m temperature_c #> 1.20045 0.34817 -0.00338 -0.00064 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} c(converged = glm_fit$converged, steps = glm_fit$iter) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> converged steps #> 1 5 ``` ::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} # scikit-learn's LogisticRegression would not match: it adds a penalty by # default (C=1.0), which Regularisation explains. statsmodels fits the model # as glm() does. glm_fit = sm.GLM(yb, sm.add_constant(d3b[inputs]), family=sm.families.Binomial()).fit() print(glm_fit.params.round(5)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> const 1.20045 #> chlorophyll_mg_m3 0.34817 #> depth_m -0.00338 #> temperature_c -0.00064 #> dtype: float64 ``` ::: ```{.python .cell-code} print({"converged": glm_fit.converged, "steps": glm_fit.fit_history["iteration"]}) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> {'converged': True, 'steps': 5} ``` ::: ::: ::: From coefficients of zero, the log loss is 0.693. The first step takes it to 0.510 and the second to 0.504; by step 5 it changes by less than 0.000001, and the coefficients match `glm()`'s. `glm()` stops when a step changes the fit by less than a set amount, and records that it has **converged**. Had the search stopped after two steps, the chlorophyll coefficient would be 0.268 instead of 0.348, 23% out, and nothing about the number would look wrong. A search that runs out of steps returns wherever it got to. R warns when that happens, but the coefficients carry no mark: the `converged` field is the place to look. ### Separation leaves no lowest point `catch_weight_kg` is the leaked column from [Avoiding information leakage](../02-marine-data/information-leakage.qmd): it is weighed from the same catch that was counted, so every station where the species was present weighs more than every station where it was absent. We use it to predict presence. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} d_leak <- survey |> select(present, catch_weight_kg) |> drop_na() |> mutate(present = fct_relevel(present, "no")) is_present <- d_leak$present == "yes" separated <- map_dfr(c(10, 25, 100), \(allowed) { fit <- glm(present ~ catch_weight_kg, data = d_leak, family = binomial, control = glm.control(maxit = allowed)) tibble( `steps allowed` = allowed, `steps taken` = fit$iter, converged = fit$converged, coefficient = coef(fit)[["catch_weight_kg"]], `training accuracy` = mean((fitted(fit) > 0.5) == is_present) ) }) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` #> Warning: glm.fit: algorithm did not converge ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` #> Warning: glm.fit: fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` #> Warning: glm.fit: algorithm did not converge ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` #> Warning: glm.fit: fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred #> Warning: glm.fit: fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} separated |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 1))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| steps allowed| steps taken|converged | coefficient| training accuracy| |-------------:|-----------:|:---------|-----------:|-----------------:| | 10| 10|FALSE | 43.4| 1| | 25| 25|FALSE | 157.9| 1| | 100| 32|TRUE | 212.8| 1|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} d_leak = survey[["present", "catch_weight_kg"]].dropna() leak_y = (d_leak["present"] == "yes").astype(float) leak_X = sm.add_constant(d_leak[["catch_weight_kg"]]) rows = [] for allowed in [10, 25, 100]: # statsmodels warns of "perfect separation"; errstate hides numpy's # overflow warnings on the way, which say the same. with np.errstate(over="ignore"), warnings.catch_warnings(): warnings.simplefilter("ignore") fit = sm.GLM(leak_y, leak_X, family=sm.families.Binomial()).fit(maxiter=allowed) rows.append({"fit": f"statsmodels, {allowed} steps allowed", "steps taken": fit.fit_history["iteration"], "converged": fit.converged, "coefficient": fit.params["catch_weight_kg"]}) # scikit-learn's LogisticRegression gives no sign at all: its default penalty # (C=1.0) stops the coefficient from walking off, so it looks ordinary. default = LogisticRegression().fit(d_leak[["catch_weight_kg"]], leak_y) rows.append({"fit": "LogisticRegression()", "steps taken": default.n_iter_[0], "converged": default.n_iter_[0] < default.max_iter, "coefficient": default.coef_[0, 0]}) pd.DataFrame(rows).round(1) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | fit | steps taken | converged | coefficient | |:-------------------------------|--------------:|:------------|--------------:| | statsmodels, 10 steps allowed | 10 | False | 43.4 | | statsmodels, 25 steps allowed | 25 | False | 157.9 | | statsmodels, 100 steps allowed | 29 | True | 189.9 | | LogisticRegression() | 9 | True | 9.3 | ::: ::: ::: This is **separation**: one input splits the two classes completely. Moving its coefficient further from zero always makes the predictions a little more confident and the log loss a little smaller, so the objective keeps falling and has no lowest point. The search walks off in that direction for as long as it is allowed: the coefficient is 43 after 10 steps and 158 after 25. Given more room, R stops after 32 steps at 213 and reports that it converged, because by then the log loss is so close to zero that a step barely changes it. Every fit classifies all the training stations correctly, and R warns that fitted probabilities of 0 or 1 occurred. So the coefficient is wherever the search gave up, not an estimate, and even a converged search can have found no real lowest point. The sign is a coefficient that keeps growing when the search is allowed more steps, with a perfect score on the training data. It does not mean the input is powerful science; it means the input gives the answer away, and in practice that is usually a leak. A penalty on the coefficients, as [Regularisation](../05-generalisation/regularisation.qmd) adds, stops the walk, which is why scikit-learn's default logistic regression, in the Python tab, returns an ordinary-looking number instead. ## Trees search one split at a time A decision tree does not walk down an objective at all. At each branch it tries every input and every split value, keeps the one that lowers the squared error most, and moves on without going back. This **greedy** search is fast, but it can miss a better tree whose first split looks worse on its own. Random forests and boosting grow many trees this way, and forests also draw stations and inputs at random, so without a set seed each run gives a slightly different model; [Reporting a model](../10-interpretation/reporting-a-model.qmd) shows how to keep a seed's draws in place. ## Each sign of a failed search has its own fix A model found by formula has nothing to check about the fit itself. A model found by search can fail in ways its coefficients do not show, and each failure leaves a sign. | Sign | What happened | What to do | | --- | --- | --- | | `converged` is `FALSE`, or a warning that the search did not converge | Ran out of steps | Allow more steps; if it still does not finish, rethink the model | | A coefficient that grows with the steps allowed, and a perfect training score | Separation: an input gives the answer away | Find that input; suspect leakage | | The objective grows with every step, or becomes `NaN` | Steps too large | Take smaller steps; [standardise the inputs](gradient-descent.qmd) | | A different answer on each run | Random choices in the fit | Set a seed to repeat it; refit without one to measure the spread | "Converged" means only that the search stopped by its own rule, and each package sets its own, so two packages fitting the same model can disagree in the third decimal place and both report success. The last check needs no software at all: are the predictions possible, with no negative counts and no probabilities outside 0 and 1? ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - **Parameters** are chosen by the fit from the data; hyperparameters, such as a tree's depth, are set before fitting and limit what the fit may do. - Linear regression under squared error has a formula: one step, exact, and the same on every run. Trying every combination instead is out of reach beyond a few parameters. - Most other models search step by step; here logistic regression settled in 5 steps from a start at zero. - A search that went wrong still prints coefficients. Stopped after two steps, the chlorophyll coefficient was 23% out and looked normal; check the `converged` flag, and treat a coefficient that grows with more steps as separation, an input that gives the answer away. - Trees choose one split at a time and never revisit it; forests and boosting add randomness on top. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Add `salinity_psu` to the formula fit and confirm it still matches `lm()`. 2. Add a copy of depth in other units, `depth_m * 2`, as a fourth input and give it to `lm()`. What does the coefficient table say, and would you have noticed without looking for it? Try the same with `solve()`. 3. Fit `glm(present ~ abundance, family = binomial)`. `present` is defined as `abundance > 0`, so abundance splits the classes exactly. How large does its coefficient grow?
